The people

Two guides, five women

Anjali and Vikram guide every module. The stories follow five women, one cast from start to finish.

Anjali

Course guide. Speaks to the woman watching, warmly and plainly.

Vikram

Course guide. Speaks to the men, and admits what he once got wrong.

Rekha

44 · line supervisor, garment factory

Started on the line; proof that it can be done.

Asha

32 · stitching operator, garment factory

Married, two children, lives with her mother-in-law.

Priya

21 · store associate, supermarket

Single, lives with her parents in a small town.

Lakshmi

38 · housekeeping, corporate office

Widowed, the earning member of her family.

Nazia

20 · patient-care assistant, hospital

Moved cities; lives in a working women's hostel.

At work everyone wears royal blue, in their sector's form. Families are shown as worried and caring, never as villains.

The look

Warm, clear, grown-up

  • Illustrated characters with realistic adult proportions and ordinary Indian faces.
  • Calm cream backgrounds and real places: the factory floor, the store, the ward, the hostel, home.
  • The narration carries the message. The screen shows only a few keywords, and captions in the learner's language.
  • No words inside the pictures, so every language uses the same illustrations.
  • Difficult moments are suggested, never shown.

Stage 1 · Before you begin · Module 1

What Is Gender Inclusion and Why Does It Affect You?

All frontline workers, men and women7 videos · ~23 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

What I say and do at work affects whether my colleague stays.

The brief

What BII asked for

Build foundational awareness of gender inclusion as something directly relevant to every worker's daily experience on the floor. Move beyond corporate jargon. Help workers understand what an inclusive workplace looks and feels like, and why it benefits everyone regardless of gender.

Gender vs. sexWhat inclusion means in a frontline contextCommon myths debunkedIndia data: where frontline women stand todayHow inclusion affects productivity, safety and team cultureWhat workers can demand from an inclusive employer
What the review added
  • Rethink the course as “what I say and do on the floor affects whether my colleague stays”: more informal and direct.
  • A short intro to basic language and phrases, with no jargon.
  • Common myths.
  • Practical examples of how inclusion plays out: banter going too far, women leaving because of limited career options.
  • What workers can do to create a more inclusive workplace (a short intro; the deeper dive comes later).

How we tell it

The Stay Battery. Every worker starts fully charged. Small words and habits drain it; a fair chance and someone who has your back charge it. It returns in every video.

Video by video

1

Small things, big exits

~3 min

Four women quietly leave four workplaces: a work coat left on a machine, a name badge on a hook, an ID card slid across a desk. Anjali and Vikram introduce the Stay Battery. Everyday moments, like a “boys, come here” huddle or a joke at her expense, drain it; the same moments done differently charge it back. When she leaves, her work lands on the rest of the shift.

2

Plain words: gender, sex and inclusion

~3 min

A handout full of long words gets folded away. Sex and gender are explained with one simple picture each: the body we are born with, and the roles we are taught. Inclusion is shown in a shift huddle: “Boys, listen” leaves Asha outside; “Team, listen” brings her in. It reaches beyond women too: the shy new boy, the older worker with a new tablet, the father asking for leave. It ends on a card of everyday word swaps.

3

Myth or fact? Six things we've all heard

~4 min

A break-room game. Six things heard on every floor are flipped one by one: “women get special treatment”, “women can't do heavy or technical work”, “it's just a joke, she laughed”, “women leave because of marriage”, “women don't want to be supervisors” and “if women get more, men get less”. Each gets one simple picture and one sourced fact, and the guides admit a myth they once believed.

4

Look around your floor: women at work in India

~3 min

Workers leaving a shift turn into a grid of people. A few sourced numbers are made human: how few women hold formal jobs with a payslip, the sectors where frontline women work, and the hours of housework many carry before and after a shift. It ends with Nazia after a night shift, on a video call with her worried mother: every woman on your floor worked hard to get there.

5

On the floor: when it goes wrong, and how to fix it

~4½ min

Three moments freeze and replay. Lunch-break banter goes too far, and a colleague changes the subject. Priya is passed over for supervisor training, and a colleague puts her name forward. Nazia stays silent about a loose drip line after being mocked for her accent, and in the redo she speaks up. Safety gear that doesn't fit shows that a floor built for everyone is safer and faster.

6

Your move: what you can do, and what you can expect

~3½ min

Three things for men: change one word, don't laugh along, share what you know. Three for women: it's okay to say “that's not okay”, ask for the training, find a buddy. Then a short checklist of what every worker can expect from a good employer, and where to go if something is missing: it's not a favour, it's a right. It closes with a quick check: pick one thing for your next shift.

7

Module 1 in two minutes

~2 min

A short recap over earlier pictures; the Stay Battery fills with each point. The four women from Video 1 are back at work. Followed by the module's scenario quiz.

★ Ready for review · Video 1 completeStage 1 · Before you begin · Module 2

Talking to Your Family About Work

Women frontline workers and new joiners8 videos · ~25 minGuides: Anjali, with Vikram

A family's “no” is usually not about you. It's about their fears.

The brief

What BII asked for

Address the single biggest hidden barrier to women entering the formal workforce: family disapproval. Equip women with practical language, real scripts and relatable stories to have these conversations confidently with husbands, in-laws and parents.

Why families resist and how to address itHandling safety and commute objectionsFraming the financial benefit for the householdScripts for husband, in-law and parent conversationsReal stories of women who navigated thisSetting expectations about hours and schedule
What the review added
  • Do no harm: pushing for money, hours or independence can lead to conflict or violence at home. Include safeguarding guidance.
  • Add unpaid care work and household duties (the “double burden”), which are often what is behind family objections.
  • Family pressure also causes exits after joining: night-shift changes, pregnancy, promotion, relocation.
  • Show different family situations: married, single, widowed, and migrant women living in hostels.
  • Think of resources that could be shared with family members, such as a short video.

How we tell it

One door, five locks. A family's “no” is a locked door, not a wall. Each lock is one fear: Safety · Reputation · Housework · Income · Change. Videos 2 to 6 open them one by one; in Video 8 the door opens. Every video gives choices, not orders, and ends with a calm safety reminder.

Video by video

1

Why families say “no” Complete

Introduces the door and its five locks · made in landscape and in vertical for phones

3 min 15 s
1

The letter at dinner

Asha's family eats together. Her offer letter stays hidden. She starts to speak, and stops.

Sometimes, the hardest interview happens at home.
2

One more “yes”

Anjali welcomes the woman watching: she has the skill, but needs one more “yes”, from home.

3

You are not alone

Many women who are trained and ready never join, or leave within months. Not because of the work.

4

The door with five locks

A family's “no” is a locked door, not a wall. Vikram asks each family question; Anjali names the fear behind it.

Not a wall. A door.

The five fears

Is it safe? · What will people say? · Who will do the housework? · Is my income not enough? · Will she change?

5

Four homes, four locks

Asha, Priya, Lakshmi and Nazia: different lives, the same question. How do I talk to my family?

6

Rekha's proof

Rekha's mother-in-law didn't speak to her for a week. Today she is proud of her.

It didn't happen in one conversation. It happened in many small ones.
7

The key message, and safety first

Fears get smaller with answers. And if talking could make someone angry or violent, safety comes first.

It's not about you. It's about their fears.
8

The first lock opens

Only the safety lock opens. Next video: “Is it safe?”

2

“Is it safe?” In production

Safety and the commute · opens the Safety lock · soft 3D look

~3½ min

Built so far: the first minute, pictured below.

1

The fear

Suresh switches off a worrying news story. Asha has asked about a job with a late shift.

Late evening travel? No.
2

It comes from love

Anjali: the fear is real, and it comes from love. Don't fight it. Answer it, with facts.

3

Five questions to ask

Before talking at home, Asha asks Rekha five questions: shift timings · transport · women on the shift · a woman guard or supervisor · who to call.

4

Write the answers down

Asha writes the answers on a small card she can keep and show at home.

Don't ask them to trust a guess. Show them a plan.

The rest of Video 2: written and ready for pictures.

  1. 5
    Show them, don't just tell them

    Asha takes Suresh along the route once: the bus stop, the gate, the security cabin. Many companies also allow a family visit. When families see other women working, the fear gets smaller.

  2. 6
    Small habits, big trust

    Sharing her live location on the way home, a “reached” message every day, her supervisor's number saved in the family's phones, and travelling with a woman colleague when she can.

  3. 7
    Far from home

    Nazia's parents live a thousand kilometres away and can't visit. She gives them a video tour of her hostel, shares the warden's number, and calls at the same time every evening. Her mother: “Now I can sleep.”

  4. 8
    Asha brings the facts home

    Asha tells Suresh what she found out: the company bus, the women on her shift, the woman guard at the gate. Then she asks him to come with her on the first day. She didn't argue; she brought facts and invited him in.

  5. 9
    Know this: night shifts

    A short note: if a night shift is ever offered, she can ask questions first, and she can say no.

  6. 10
    Close

    “Fear needs answers, not arguments.” A calm safety reminder, then a pointer to Video 3: money, as “us”, not “me”.

3

“What will we gain?”

Talking about money as a family · opens the Income lock

~3½ min
  1. 1
    Lakshmi's kitchen table

    A school-fee notice in one hand, a small box of coins in the other. For Lakshmi, working is not a choice. For many families money is delicate: “Is my income not enough?”

  2. 2
    Talk about the goal, not the salary

    A family notebook, “Our family plan”: school fees, the loan, savings for emergencies. Asha first thanks Suresh for his hard work, then shows how her job gets the family there faster, together.

  3. 3
    More than a salary

    What a formal job brings the whole household: medical cover for the family, savings with the company adding its share, maternity leave, and a fixed salary date. Ask HR which ones apply.

  4. 4
    What will people say?

    A neighbour teases Priya's father at the tea stall. Six months later, the same neighbour asks him if there's a job for his own daughter.

  5. 5
    Agree on the money together

    Home, children, savings and a small personal amount, agreed before she joins. And a calm note: if anyone takes her salary or card by force, that is not okay, and Video 7 can help.

Not “my salary”. “Our goal”.

4

“Who will do the housework?”

The double burden · opens the Housework lock

~3½ min
  1. 1
    Asha's 18-hour day

    Her day runs fast from 5 am to 11 pm: cooking, children, the bus, the factory, homework, dinner, dishes. First shift paid; second shift unpaid.

  2. 2
    The question behind the “no”

    For many families the real worry is: if she works, who will do everything at home? A simple picture shows how much more unpaid work women carry each day.

  3. 3
    A home roster

    The factory's shift roster turns into a roster on the kitchen wall. The family lists every task and shares them out.

  4. 4
    Ask with respect

    Asha asks Amma to look after the children in the afternoon, and Suresh to do the school drop. Start with one task, not ten, and say thank you.

  5. 5
    Ask your workplace too

    Ask HR about a crèche, and talk to the supervisor about shift options before ever thinking of quitting.

Housework is real work. It doesn't have to be one woman's work.

5

The conversation

Husband, in-laws, parents · opens the Reputation lock

~5 min
  1. 1
    The four Ts

    Four homes, four doors. Four simple rules before any conversation: Time, Tone, Truth, Trial.

  2. 2
    Asha and Suresh

    She asks for his advice, respects his role, brings a plan for the children, and asks for a one-month trial. “One month. Let's see.”

  3. 3
    Asha and Amma

    With elders, respect and involvement work better than reasons. Amma becomes part of the plan, and the evening tea waits in a flask.

  4. 4
    Priya and her parents

    Her mother becomes her ally, and her store manager offers to meet the family. Her father agrees to come and see the store on Saturday.

  5. 5
    Lakshmi and Nazia

    Lakshmi asks her brother-in-law for his blessing, not his permission. Nazia builds her parents' trust on a phone call, every evening.

  6. 6
    If the answer is still “no”

    “Not now” is not “never”. Give it time. But if a “no” comes with threats or anger, her safety comes first.

Time. Tone. Truth. Trial.

6

Hours, shifts and the changes ahead

After joining · opens the Change lock

~3½ min
  1. 1
    “You said 5 o'clock”

    Asha gets home at 7:15. The shift ended on time, but nobody planned for the bus, the traffic and the walk.

  2. 2
    Tell your family the full picture

    Full hours including travel, overtime, the weekly off, the salary date, and the harder first months. Promise less, deliver more.

  3. 3
    Four turning points

    A night shift (Asha), a pregnancy (Priya), a promotion (Lakshmi), a transfer (Nazia). For each: what to ask HR and what to say at home.

  4. 4
    Before you resign

    Rekha: “Before you resign, come and talk to me. Most problems have a solution you haven't heard about yet.”

Before you resign, talk to us.

7

When talking isn't safe

A calm, protective video

~3 min
  1. 1
    A gentle start

    A short note on what this video covers. A quiet room, a window, a plant on the sill. No one is shown being hurt.

  2. 2
    Warning signs

    Simple icons, one at a time, for the signs that talking about work may not be safe right now.

  3. 3
    Steps to stay safe

    Tell one person you trust, keep important papers safe, remember one number by heart, agree a code word, and keep a little money aside if you safely can.

  4. 4
    Where to get help

    Helplines and local support centres, the protection the law gives, and HR or a supervisor in confidence.

  5. 5
    Your choice

    Whatever she decides is her choice, and it is never her fault. The plant on the sill grows a new leaf.

You are not alone. Help is one call away.

8

Real stories

Four real women · the door opens

~3 min
  1. 1
    Four real women

    Women from the field (married, single, widowed, and one living in a hostel far from home) tell how their family's “no” turned into support. Names are changed.

  2. 2
    The door opens

    Back at the door from Video 1. Asha, Priya, Lakshmi and Nazia each turn a key. The door opens onto a bright workplace, and Rekha welcomes them in.

  3. 3
    Close

    Your family's fears are real. So are your dreams. Then the module summary and quiz.

Every “yes” started with one conversation.

Stage 1 · Before you begin · Module 3.0

How You Can Create an Inclusive Culture

Male frontline workers6 videos · ~22 minGuides: Vikram, with Anjali

Staying quiet is also a choice. One calm move changes the room.

The brief

Proposed in the review

Understand how your behaviour at work and at home can impact women's lives, and how to become an ally.

Men's worries: “women will take our jobs”, “they get special treatment”Supporting the women in your family to workSpeaking up when you see inequalities
What the review added
  • Suggested adding this module: otherwise the responsibility sits with women only.
  • Address men's worries (“women will take our jobs”, “they get special treatment”).
  • Add “supporting the women in your family to work”: many husbands and brothers of potential women workers are frontline workers themselves.
  • Speaking up when you see inequalities.

How we tell it

Vikram leads, speaking man to man. The story stays on the garment floor with Ravi and Mahesh, and goes home with Ravi.

Video by video

1

Will women take our jobs?

~5 min

Vikram sits with Ravi and Mahesh at the tea break and takes their worries seriously. Simple facts show the work is growing, and that fair rules, like better tools or a safer bus, help everyone on the shift.

2

Where's the line?

~4 min

Three quick floor moments, each paused on three questions: Is it welcome? Is it repeated? Is it about her body or her gender? The learner decides whether it is fun or not, then sees what happens next.

3

Stepping in without a fight

~5 min

The same scene played four ways: say something, change the subject, get help, or check on her afterwards. Each is calm, quick and safe for the man who steps in.

4

Allyship at home

~4 min

Ravi's wife has a job offer. He takes on the morning school run and backs her when his mother objects. Ends with a short video he can share with his family.

5

My one step

~2 min

Each man picks one ally action for the coming week.

6

Module in two minutes

~2 min

A short recap and a scenario quiz.

Stage 2 · Getting in · Module 3

Finding the Right Job for You

All frontline workers (especially women)5 videos · ~22 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

A good job fits your life and is real. Check both before you say yes.

The brief

What BII asked for

Equip workers entering formal employment for the first time with the knowledge to evaluate job opportunities critically. Build job-search confidence and awareness of platforms, safety signals, and rights during hiring.

How to evaluate a job: safety, pay, flexibility, commuteUnderstanding job descriptionsRed flags and green flags in a job offerUsing platforms like GoBetterQuestions to ask a recruiterWhat good onboarding looks likeIs this workplace safe for me?
What the review added
  • Make the target group clear: either an optional jobseeker module, or reframe it as “Is this job right for me, and how do I make it work?”
  • Add a checklist of things to think about (facilities, transport, complaints committee, crèche, shift timings), making clear it is each woman's choice which ones matter to her.
  • Add: spotting fake jobs and illegal fees; questions employers are not allowed to ask (marriage, pregnancy plans); how to check a company or job offer is real.
  • Take out “what good onboarding looks like”: a woman has little say over it.

How we tell it

Priya, choosing her first store job, carries the module.

Video by video

1

What matters to me?

~5 min

Priya has two job offers. She builds her own checklist: shift timings, transport, toilets, a crèche, a complaints committee. Anjali is clear that which ones matter is her choice.

2

Reading a job post and an offer

~4 min

A job post read line by line: pay, hours, place, benefits. Then the offer letter, and what must be in writing before she says yes.

3

Red flags: fake jobs and wrong questions

~6 min

Three short traps: a “registration fee”, a job that is too good to be true, and an interviewer who asks about marriage and pregnancy plans. How to check a company is real, and what to say to a question that isn't allowed.

4

Questions to ask a recruiter

~5 min

Priya asks three questions before she accepts, and the recruiter is glad she did. Asking shows you are serious.

5

Module in two minutes

~2 min

A short recap and a scenario quiz.

Stage 2 · Getting in · Module 4

Building the Skills Employers Want

All frontline workers5 videos · ~22 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

You already have skills. Name them, then grow one.

The brief

What BII asked for

Help frontline workers understand the skills landscape and build a personal upskilling roadmap. Break the belief that their current skill level is fixed. Show concretely how small accessible steps lead to better jobs and better pay.

In-demand skills by sectorFree and low-cost certificationsUsing your current job to build your profileDemonstrating skills without formal educationOvercoming the confidence gap in skill-buildingHow GoBetter connects skills to jobs
What the review added
  • Show women in non-traditional, higher-paid roles (forklift, machine operator, EV technician, warehouse supervisor).
  • Replace “confidence gap” with “You already have skills”: count skills from managing a household, informal work and caregiving, and translate them to the work context.

How we tell it

Lakshmi, who runs a home and a housekeeping team, carries the module.

Video by video

1

You already have skills

~5 min

Lakshmi says she has “no skills”. Then we watch her week: budgeting, planning, caring for her family, guiding new staff. Each one becomes a work word: planning, handling money, leading a team.

2

Jobs that are growing

~5 min

Women in roles many people think are for men: forklift driver, machine operator, EV technician, warehouse supervisor. One of them tells, in her own voice, how she got there.

3

Learn for free or low cost

~5 min

How to find a short free or low-cost course that fits around a shift and a family, shown step by step on a phone.

4

Your 3-step skill plan

~5 min

Lakshmi picks one skill, one course and one start date, and tells her children about it.

5

Module in two minutes

~2 min

A short recap and a scenario quiz.

Stage 2 · Getting in · Module 5

Using AI to Find Jobs, Learn, and Get Ahead

All frontline workers6 videos · ~27 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

Ask in your own words, and never share what is yours alone.

The brief

What BII asked for

Democratise access to AI tools for workers who may never have used them. Give practical, hands-on guidance on using AI chatbots and voice tools to improve job search, understand rights, prepare for interviews, and solve everyday work problems, starting from zero digital confidence.

What AI is and how it helps (zero jargon)Using WhatsApp AI bots to search jobs and ask questionsVoice AI: ask with your voiceAI for interview prepHow to ask AI about your rightsSafety: what not to sharePractical prompt examples in Hindi and local languages
What the review added
  • Asking AI about rights: make clear it is not legal advice, only a basic understanding.
  • Add prompts for finding the right job portals, or a job that fits your skills.
  • Add fraud prevention.

How we tell it

Nazia, using her phone in her own language, carries the module.

Video by video

1

What is AI? (no jargon)

~3 min

A plain-words picture of an AI assistant: a helper that answers questions in your language, and can sometimes be wrong.

2

Ask with your voice

~6 min

Nazia asks a question out loud in her own language, on her phone and on WhatsApp. No typing and no English needed.

3

AI for jobs and interviews

~6 min

Starter questions to find jobs that fit her skills and the right job sites, then a practice interview where the assistant plays the interviewer.

4

Your rights, and the limits

~4 min

Nazia asks about her leave. The answer helps her understand, but it is not legal advice, so she checks with HR.

5

Stay safe with AI and online

~6 min

Never share OTPs, ID numbers or bank details. Three quick tests: spot the scam.

6

Module in two minutes

~2 min

A short recap and a scenario quiz.

Stage 2 · Getting in · Module 6

Your Network Is Your Biggest Asset

All frontline workers (especially women)6 videos · ~22 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

A few trusted people can get you in, and keep you in.

The brief

What BII asked for

Build understanding of how informal and formal referral networks drive career opportunity. Give workers tools to build their own peer community, and connect this to real referral benefits on GoBetter.

What a network means for a frontline workerHow referrals work and how to use themReferring other women and earning from itGoBetter network and referral featuresBuilding trust-based relationships at workPeer learning
What the review added
  • Women's networks tend to be smaller, more family-based and limited by restrictions on going out: acknowledge that.
  • Peer networks also matter for staying in the job: women leave when they feel isolated.
  • Add safety when networking (sharing numbers, groups with unknown people).
  • Recruit women in groups: women deployed together feel safer and are more likely to stay.

How we tell it

Priya and her colleagues at the store carry the module.

Video by video

1

Why your network matters

~4 min

Most jobs come through people. Priya's brother hears about jobs at the tea stall; her own circle is smaller, and that is not her fault. Small steps can grow it.

2

Your trust circle at work

~5 min

Priya picks two or three people at the store: a buddy, a senior, a friend from training. Who she calls when a day is hard.

3

Referrals: help a friend, help yourself

~5 min

Priya refers a friend through the company's referral programme, and both of them benefit.

4

Networking safely

~4 min

Which numbers to share, which groups to join, and when to leave a group.

5

Go together

~2 min

Two friends apply, join and stay together. A real woman tells why it helped.

6

Module in two minutes

~2 min

A short recap and a scenario quiz.

Stage 3 · Navigating work · Module 90D

Your First 90 Days

New joiners6 videos · ~17 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

Don't leave quietly. Ask early.

The brief

Proposed in the review

Help people ease into formal employment and stay: most attrition happens in the first 90 days.

Adjusting to formal work, shifts and rulesWho to ask for whatBuddy and peer supportHandling a tough first weekWhen to raise a concernTalking to family about how it's going
What the review added
  • Suggested adding this module: most attrition happens in the first 90 days.

Stage 3 · Navigating work · Module 7

Know Your Rights as a Worker

All frontline workers6 videos · ~27 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

Know what you're owed, and climb the ladder to claim it.

The brief

What BII asked for

Ensure every worker knows their fundamental legal entitlements in clear, actionable language. Not just “you have rights” but “here is exactly what you are owed and how to claim it if it isn't given.”

Minimum wage and reading your salary slipMaternity and paternity entitlementsPOSH Act basics for all gendersLeave rights: casual, sick, earnedSafety standards your employer must maintainEqual pay basicsHow to raise a formal complaintWomen: maternity, crèche, night-shift protections
What the review added
  • Split into “rights everyone has” and “extra protections for women”. Mark which rights apply to permanent, contract and gig workers.
  • Add an escalation ladder: supervisor → HR → ICC → Local Committee or labour department → helplines (181) and the SHe-Box portal. Add protection against retaliation.
  • Add workplace facilities rights (toilets, rest and changing areas, crèche threshold) and equal pay for the same work.

How we tell it

Lakshmi, employed through a facility-management company, carries the module.

Video by video

1

Your type of work, your rights

~4 min

Permanent, contract or gig? Lakshmi finds out which she is, and which rights follow.

2

Rights everyone has

~6 min

Wages and the payslip, leave, safe work and equal pay for the same work, in plain words with simple pictures.

3

Extra protections for women

~5 min

Maternity, crèche, night shifts, toilets and rest areas: not favours, the law. With a real woman's voice.

4

The law against sexual harassment at work

~4 min

What counts as harassment, for all genders, and who the complaints committee is. Short scenarios.

5

The rights ladder

~6 min

One step at a time: supervisor, HR, the complaints committee, the local committee or labour department, then helplines. And no one may punish you for using it.

6

Module in two minutes

~2 min

A short recap and a scenario quiz.

Stage 3 · Navigating work · Module 8

Your Safety: At Work, On the Commute, and Online

All frontline workers (especially women)6 videos · ~22 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

Being safe is your right, not your job to manage alone.

The brief

What BII asked for

Address the full safety landscape: physical safety on the floor, commute safety, and digital safety, with practical tools and contacts workers can use immediately. Make safety feel manageable, not overwhelming.

Workplace safety: what your employer must provideResponding to unsafe situations on the floorCommute safety: practical steps and appsNight-shift protections for womenWhat to do if you face or witness harassmentEmergency contacts and helplinesDigital safety: protecting your identity online
What the review added
  • Personal-safety tips (“be careful”, “avoid…”) put the responsibility on women and can feed the restrictive norms families use to keep women from working.
  • Put the employer's duties first and personal tips second, so it reads as “your right to be safe”, not “your job to avoid danger”.

How we tell it

Nazia on night duty and Asha on the late bus. The employer's duty always comes first; personal tips second.

Video by video

1

Your right to be safe

~5 min

What the employer must provide: transport, lighting, toilets and safety gear. The employer's duty comes first.

2

Unsafe on the floor

~4 min

A spill, a broken guard, a machine left running: stop, tell, report.

3

Getting to and from work

~4 min

Asha asks for safe transport on a late shift, and uses simple tools on the way home.

4

If you face or see harassment

~4 min

With a gentle note at the start. What a woman can do if it happens to her, what a colleague can do if they see it, and where to get help.

5

Online safety and your emergency card

~3 min

Protect your photos and ID online, and save the emergency card in your phone.

6

Module in two minutes

~2 min

A short recap and a scenario quiz.

Stage 4 · Growing · Module 9

Financial Independence: Your Money, Your Control

All frontline workers6 videos · ~22 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

Your own money, planned well, protects your whole family.

The brief

What BII asked for

Build financial awareness and ownership, especially for workers entering formal paid employment for the first time. Connect earning to owning. Help workers understand, manage, and grow their income rather than simply receiving it and handing it over.

Reading your salary slip line by lineOpening and using a bank accountUPI and digital payments basicsBasic savings habitsUnderstanding deductions: PF, ESI, TDSNot letting others control your salaryWomen: financial independence as protection from domestic pressure
What the review added
  • Reframe as “Your money, your family's future”: present her own account and savings as good for the household, with confidential help for anyone facing coercion.
  • Add scam awareness, an emergency fund, how to use insurance, and PF/UAN basics.
  • Introduce micro-habits, such as saving ₹50 a week.

How we tell it

Lakshmi and Asha, planning with their families, carry the module.

3

~4 min

4

~4 min

What basic insurance does, and three money scams to spot.

5

Your money, your family's future

~3 min

Her savings shown as good for the whole family, and where to get confidential help if anyone controls her money.

Stage 4 · Growing · Module 10

Your Career Does Not Stop Here

All frontline workers (especially women)5 videos · ~22 minGuides: Anjali and Vikram

Your current job is a step, not the ceiling.

The brief

What BII asked for

Break the deeply held belief that the current role is the ceiling. Show a clear, credible, inspiring pathway from today's role to tomorrow's opportunity. Give concrete first steps to start moving.

Career pathways: worker to team lead to supervisorReal stories of workers who moved upHow to ask for a promotionBuilding a skills-based case for your growthUsing GoBetter to discover career pathsOvercoming the “I'm not ready” mindsetA personal development plan on a frontline schedule
What the review added
  • Add what supervisors look for; how to ask for training, acting roles and shift changes; telling the family about a promotion.
  • Feature women team leads and supervisors as role models.

How we tell it

Asha takes her first step towards Rekha's role.

Asha asks Rekha for training and an acting role: one thing, one reason, at the right time.

4

A simple growth plan, and a conversation at home about what a promotion will mean for the family.
